paragraphs: Improving a diffusion model for a particular task can require optimizing two linked decisions: how the model is trained or adapted, and which settings make that process work best. The paper formulates this dependency as generative bilevel optimization. Conventional approaches encounter difficulties because diffusion processes involve probability distributions in an infinite-dimensional space and can require expensive repeated sampling.

The authors develop a first-order framework for two settings. For adapting a pretrained model, they combine a lower-level solver that uses inference only with an upper-level gradient estimator designed to use samples efficiently. For training from scratch, they reformulate the lower-level problem and construct a tractable gradient estimator to optimize the noise schedule.

These contributions make the nested optimization structure explicit while providing different computational solutions for adaptation and initial training. The framework has theoretical support, and the reported experiments outperform existing fine-tuning and hyperparameter-search baselines. The findings support treating these settings as connected optimization problems whose dependencies can be handled directly.
icml-2025-a-first-order-generative-bilev.tldr: A first-order bilevel framework makes diffusion-model adaptation and noise-schedule optimization computationally tractable, with reported improvements over existing baselines.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how interactions between brain regions could support efficient learning when a decision unfolds through space. The authors build models of a neuroscience task involving a binary decision, combining grid and place cells associated with the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus with a recurrent cortical network that selects actions.

They compare reinforcement-learning agents whose brain models use different interaction architectures. This lets them examine how changing information flow affects both learning performance and internal neural representations. Among the alternatives considered, the strongest architecture gives grid cells both self-movement velocity and increments of decision evidence, allowing those signals to be encoded jointly.

That architecture achieves the best learning efficiency while most closely reproducing experimental observations in the comparison. The results suggest a useful structured design for reinforcement learning and motivate a biological prediction: effective spatial decision-making requires grid cells to jointly encode position and evidence. This is presented as a testable prediction from the models, providing a specific target for future neurophysiological experiments.
icml-2025-a-multi-region-brain-model-to-.tldr: Comparing brain-inspired learning architectures suggests that jointly encoding movement and decision evidence can improve spatial decision-making.

paragraphs: ABNet addresses a difficult combination of requirements for robot learning: control policies should be trainable, robust to noisy observations, and supported by formal safety guarantees. The paper identifies scalability, training difficulty, inefficiency, and unstable outputs as obstacles in existing safe-learning methods, especially when those methods must control physical robots.

Its architecture places safety barriers explicitly inside a closed-form model. Multiple heads can learn safe control policies from different features, with each attending to a particular part of the observation. This organization avoids having to construct one large model directly for a complex task and is intended to make training easier while maintaining stable outputs.

The authors formally prove safety guarantees for ABNet and demonstrate the approach in two-dimensional obstacle avoidance, robot manipulation, and vision-based autonomous driving. They report stronger robustness and guarantees than existing models. The architecture also offers a possible route toward incrementally larger safe foundation models, although that scaling direction is described as potential rather than an already demonstrated outcome.
icml-2025-abnet-adaptive-explicit-barrie.tldr: ABNet combines explicit safety barriers with multiple policy heads to support provably safe robot learning and more robust control.

paragraphs: This study asks whether more attractive AI-generated images are harder for detection models to recognize. Its results challenge that intuition: among the text-to-image generators examined, images receiving higher quality scores from human preference models tend to be easier for existing detectors to identify. Here, quality refers specifically to those preference-model scores.

The authors investigate both the prompts used to create images and the images’ visual characteristics. Shorter prompts tend to produce images with higher preference scores that are also easier to detect. Clustering and regression analyses further show that saturation, contrast, and texture richness collectively affect both quality scores and detection accuracy.

The study then turns these relationships into a practical detection improvement. Regression-model predictions guide which patches of an image are supplied to an off-the-shelf detector, improving performance across different generators and datasets. The findings indicate that perceived appeal and machine detection difficulty can move in different directions, and that selecting informative image regions can help existing detectors.
icml-2025-are-high-quality-ai-generated-.tldr: AI-generated images with higher preference-model quality scores tend to be easier to detect, and that relationship can improve detector inputs.

paragraphs: Causal abstraction connects a detailed model of cause and effect to a simpler description. A difficulty arises when simplification discards information: two different interventions can become the same high-level intervention even though their effects differ. Existing definitions commonly depend on an abstract invariance condition that rules out this mismatch, limiting their treatment of lossy representations.

The paper introduces projected abstractions to accommodate that situation. It explains how to construct a projected abstraction from a low-level causal model and translate equivalent causal questions into the high-level representation. These questions cover observations, interventions, and counterfactuals, so the framework addresses more than prediction from observed correlations.

Because the true low-level model is rarely available, the authors also prove a graphical criterion for identifying and estimating high-level causal queries from limited low-level data. Experiments with high-dimensional images demonstrate the effectiveness of the resulting models. The contribution broadens the formal treatment of causal simplification to representations that merge causally distinct low-level possibilities.
icml-2025-causal-abstraction-inference-u.tldr: Projected abstractions extend causal modeling to lossy representations that merge low-level interventions with different effects.

paragraphs: Chameleon tackles the choice of how much training data to draw from different domains. Those proportions affect language-model generalization, but existing methods can require expensive calculations and another round of proxy training when the available data changes. The paper proposes computing domain weights through relationships in a learned embedding space.

The method first represents domains with embeddings and builds a matrix describing their affinities. It then derives leverage scores that determine the data mixture, giving greater weight to domains that share common representations. When new data arrives, the framework can transfer by computing embeddings for the new domains, making the weighting procedure adaptable.

Experiments cover pretraining, changing datasets, and fine-tuning. The calculated weights improve pretraining-domain performance using a fraction of existing methods’ compute. Transfer to new data improves few-shot reasoning accuracy without proxy retraining. During fine-tuning, domain reweighting improves test perplexity over uniform mixing on every evaluated domain. Together, these results support embedding relationships as a useful basis for efficient, reusable mixture decisions.
icml-2025-chameleon-a-flexible-data-mixi.tldr: Chameleon uses domain embeddings and leverage scores to choose effective training mixtures that adapt to new data without proxy retraining.

paragraphs: Drag-based image editing lets a user move selected points on an object toward desired locations. Existing diffusion-based methods repeatedly adjust an input feature representation and track those points. The paper identifies two obstacles: the representation may inadequately support motion supervision, and searching for the moving points can consume substantial computation.

DragLoRA introduces low-rank adaptation modules into this editing process and optimizes them online. An additional denoising score distillation loss keeps the adapted model’s output aligned with the original model. The updated adapters also reshape the input features, providing more stable and accurate representations for the subsequent motion-supervision steps.

The framework adds an adaptive optimization scheme that switches between two modes to improve efficiency while preserving precision. Experiments report significant gains in both editing control and computational efficiency. The central contribution is to connect model adaptation with feature adjustment during an edit, so that the representation used to guide movement can improve alongside the editing process itself.
icml-2025-draglora-online-optimization-o.tldr: DragLoRA adapts a diffusion model during drag-based editing to improve movement precision and computational efficiency.

paragraphs: SignSGD is useful both as an optimizer and as a simplified setting for studying adaptive methods such as Adam. Researchers broadly understand that it changes the geometry of optimization and reshapes gradient noise, but those descriptions do not by themselves quantify what happens. This paper develops a solvable high-dimensional analysis to make those effects precise.

The authors derive a limiting stochastic differential equation and an ordinary differential equation describing risk. Their framework separates four effects: the effective learning rate, noise compression, diagonal preconditioning, and gradient-noise reshaping. It also quantifies how these effects depend on the distributions of the data and noise.

The resulting analysis agrees with experimental observations while explaining their distributional dependence more explicitly. Its theoretical conclusions are established in a high-dimensional limit, which is central to the framework. The paper closes with a conjecture about extending the results to Adam; that proposed extension is a direction for further work rather than an established result of the analysis.
icml-2025-exact-risk-curves-of-signsgd-i.tldr: A high-dimensional analysis quantifies how SignSGD changes learning rates, preconditioning, and gradient noise as data and noise distributions vary.

paragraphs: GuardAgent checks whether another language-model agent’s actions comply with a supplied safety request. Its approach turns the request into an executable checking procedure. This addresses the need to apply safety rules dynamically as agents take actions, with the guardrail itself using language-model reasoning to interpret what should be enforced.

The process has two stages. GuardAgent first produces a task plan from the safety request, then converts that plan into guardrail code. Executing the code provides deterministic enforcement of the implemented checks. Both stages draw on demonstrations retrieved from a memory of previous tasks, giving the reasoning component relevant examples of earlier guardrail work.

The authors introduce two benchmarks: EICU-AC for healthcare-agent access control and Mind2Web-SC for web-agent safety policies. GuardAgent achieves guardrail accuracies above 98% and 83%, respectively, and effectively moderates violating actions in those evaluations. The results support combining reasoning with executable checks, while the measured accuracies distinguish overall guardrail performance from the determinism of code execution.
icml-2025-guardagent-safeguard-llm-agent.tldr: GuardAgent translates safety requests into executable guardrail code, achieving strong measured accuracy for healthcare and web agents.

paragraphs: KIND changes pretraining so that a model can later be separated into useful components. The motivation is twofold: fixed model sizes complicate deployment under different resource budgets, and transferring a pretrained model can hurt performance when its original tasks differ substantially from the target task. Decomposable knowledge offers a way to address both issues.

The method uses singular value decomposition as a structural constraint. Each basic component combines a column vector, a singular value, and a row vector. During training, a class gate directs knowledge into two component types: learngenes capture knowledge shared across classes, while tailors capture knowledge specific to particular classes.

Experiments show that these components can be separated and recombined for deployments with different resource constraints. For tasks involving large domain shifts, transferring only learngenes and pairing them with randomly initialized tailors mitigates the shift. The findings connect model structure to transfer decisions: deployment can select reusable knowledge and avoid carrying over class-specific components that are less suitable for a new task.
icml-2025-kind-knowledge-integration-and.tldr: KIND pretrains decomposable models whose shared and class-specific components can be recombined for deployment and more selective transfer.

paragraphs: Latent Diffusion Planning addresses imitation learning’s dependence on large collections of expert demonstrations. It divides the task into planning future states and predicting the actions needed to move between states. This separation lets the two components learn from different kinds of data, including demonstrations without action labels and behavior that is not optimal.

The system first learns a compact representation of image observations using a variational autoencoder. A planner then forecasts future states in this latent space, while an inverse dynamics model predicts actions. Both components are trained with diffusion objectives. The planner can use action-free demonstrations, and the inverse dynamics model can benefit from suboptimal data.

This modular design extracts supervision from data that the compared imitation-learning approaches cannot exploit. In simulated visual robot-manipulation tasks, LDP outperforms state-of-the-art alternatives under that data advantage. The result supports separating planning from action prediction when additional observations or imperfect behavior are available, expanding the useful training material beyond complete expert demonstrations.
icml-2025-latent-diffusion-planning-for-.tldr: Latent Diffusion Planning separates planning from action prediction so imitation learning can use action-free demonstrations and suboptimal data.

paragraphs: Predicting electronic properties becomes difficult when a material contains disorder, interfaces, or defects. Such structures can require large unit cells containing thousands of atoms, making density functional theory calculations prohibitively expensive. The paper develops a graph neural network for learning the electronic Hamiltonian of these extended materials, moving beyond small or readily repeating structures.

The network is strictly local and equivariant. Its key scaling mechanism is augmented partitioning, which allows training on arbitrarily large structures while preserving local atomic environments across partition boundaries. Preserving those environments matters because dividing a structure should retain the neighborhood information that the local model needs.

The demonstrations include systems with up to 3,000 atoms, more than 500,000 graph edges, and 28 million nonzero Hamiltonian entries representing orbital interactions. Reported errors in the eigenvalue spectra are at most 0.53%. These results extend learned electronic-property prediction to structurally complex materials, with partitioning serving as the bridge between local modeling and large atomic systems.
icml-2025-learning-the-electronic-hamilt.tldr: A local equivariant graph network uses augmented partitioning to predict electronic Hamiltonians for complex materials containing thousands of atoms.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a model can learn individual, interpretable concepts from images and text, together with the relationships between them. Such concepts could provide more precise control over image generation and editing. The theoretical challenge is establishing when the underlying concepts can be identified from multimodal data rather than remaining entangled in an opaque representation.

The authors formulate concepts as latent variables and use a graphical model to describe their interactions across modalities. They establish conditions for component-wise identifiability under flexible, nonparametric assumptions that accommodate both continuous and discrete modalities. The guarantee concerns recovery of individual concept components under those conditions.

Building on this theory, the authors develop a text-to-image model that explicitly learns textual and visual concepts with sparse connections between them. This structure enables generation and editing at the level of individual concepts. Empirical evaluations report better text-to-image performance, controllability, and interpretability than existing methods. The contribution links conditions for identifiable representations to a concrete architecture for controlling generated images.
icml-2025-learning-vision-and-language-c.tldr: The paper establishes conditions for identifying multimodal concepts and uses them to build more controllable, interpretable image generation.

paragraphs: LoRA-Gen aims to specialize small language models running at the edge by using a larger model in the cloud. Its starting point is that increasing model scale does not fully resolve the efficiency and effectiveness challenges of domain-specific tasks, particularly when the deployed model must remain small.

Given a task description, the cloud model generates low-rank adaptation parameters for the edge model. A reparameterization step merges these parameters into the smaller model, enabling flexible specialization. The approach transfers knowledge between models and reduces the input context length needed by the specialized model, improving its inference efficiency.

The paper reports that specialization without specialized training outperforms conventional LoRA fine-tuning. Its results include competitive reasoning accuracy and a 2.1-fold speedup with TinyLLaMA-1.1B, plus a reported compression ratio of 10.1 with Gemma-2B on intelligent-agent tasks. These findings support generating adaptations from task descriptions as a practical way to connect cloud-model capabilities with smaller deployed models.
icml-2025-lora-gen-specializing-large-la.tldr: LoRA-Gen uses a cloud language model to generate task-specific adapters for smaller edge models, reducing context needs and improving inference efficiency.

paragraphs: Minerva evaluates how effectively language models use information in their context. The paper argues that manually constructed, static benchmarks can be difficult to interpret and susceptible to overfitting. A failed test may reveal that something went wrong without showing which memory capability was responsible, limiting the usefulness of the result.

The proposed framework automatically generates tests for distinct operations on context memory. These include searching, recalling, editing, matching, and comparing information. It also tests basic operations when inputs are organized into separate blocks and the ability to maintain state while working with memory. This broadens evaluation beyond finding a hidden item or retrieving a stored value.

Minerva additionally combines these operations into more complex tasks. Testing both individual capabilities and their combinations creates a more detailed picture of how a model handles contextual information. The contribution is an interpretable assessment framework: its task structure is designed to make memory failures more informative and to expose difficulties that search-focused benchmarks may leave unexamined.
icml-2025-minerva-a-programmable-memory-.tldr: Minerva automatically generates interpretable tests of language-model context use, covering memory operations beyond simple retrieval.

paragraphs: MUDDFormer changes how information moves between Transformer layers. The paper targets limitations of residual connections and proposes dense connections whose weights adapt to the current hidden states. This makes cross-layer information flow responsive to what the network is processing at each sequence position.

The method generates separate connection weights for a block’s query, key, value, and residual input streams. Each stream can therefore receive its own dynamically weighted combination of cross-layer information. The authors present these connections as compatible with any Transformer architecture, allowing the same modification to be applied across different model designs.

Language-modeling experiments across architectures and scales report performance comparable to Transformers trained with 1.8 to 2.4 times as much compute. MUDDPythia-2.8B matches Pythia-6.9B on pretraining perplexity and downstream tasks, and rivals Pythia-12B in five-shot settings. The reported overhead is only 0.23% more parameters and 0.4% more computation. These comparisons suggest that more adaptive use of existing layers can deliver substantial gains with very small architectural overhead.
icml-2025-muddformer-breaking-residual-b.tldr: MUDDFormer dynamically weights cross-layer connections for separate Transformer input streams, improving language-model performance with little added computation.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation supplies a language model with documents selected from a corpus. This paper examines whether an attacker can manipulate that selection by inserting poisoned documents. The focus is the retrieval system, a component whose behavior determines which external information reaches the generation process.

Across 225 combinations of corpora, retrievers, queries, and targeted information in medical question answering, the authors find vulnerability to universal poisoning attacks. Poisoned documents can contain varied targeted information, including personally identifiable information, and can be retrieved by different users when they submit attacker-specified queries. That query condition is part of the reported attack behavior.

The authors connect the vulnerability to a pattern in the embedding difference between a query and a poisoned document: the document can retain high similarity to the query despite containing the targeted information. They use this finding to develop a detection-based defense. Experiments across question-answering domains report excellent detection rates in nearly all cases, supporting the defense’s effectiveness in the evaluated settings.
icml-2025-on-the-vulnerability-of-applyi.tldr: The study finds query-conditioned poisoning vulnerabilities in RAG retrieval and develops an embedding-informed defense with strong reported detection performance.

paragraphs: Automated neural architecture search typically evaluates many candidate networks, making design expensive. This paper proposes generating high-performing architectures directly, without a search-and-evaluation loop during generation. The approach uses prior knowledge about which architectural components contribute to performance to guide a diffusion model.

To construct that prior knowledge, the authors first quantify the contribution of individual components to an architecture’s overall performance. The diffusion model then uses this information to generate architectures for different computational tasks. This connects component-level performance knowledge with a generative model of network designs.

Experiments on new search spaces report higher accuracy than state-of-the-art methods. The paper reports architecture generation requiring 0.004 GPU days, with resulting architectures reaching 76.1% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet and 97.56% on CIFAR-10. It also finds competitive architectures in unseen spaces including TransNAS-Bench-101 and NATS-Bench. These findings support the usefulness of the guidance beyond one search space; the stated GPU cost concerns architecture generation.
icml-2025-prior-knowledge-guided-neural-.tldr: A diffusion model guided by component-level performance knowledge generates competitive neural architectures without a generation-time search loop.

paragraphs: A calibrated language model’s confidence should reflect how often its answers are correct. This paper examines why preference alignment can disrupt that relationship. The authors observe that preference collapse extends into calibration, producing overconfidence, even though pretrained models are typically well calibrated before alignment.

They show that fine-tuning with domain-specific knowledge is important for reducing overconfidence. To understand when calibration can improve without harming performance, they distinguish calibratable and non-calibratable regimes using bounds on Expected Calibration Error. Within the calibratable regime, their calibration-aware fine-tuning approach achieves proper calibration while preserving model performance.

Further fine-tuning for better performance can move models into the non-calibratable regime. For this situation, the authors develop an Expected Calibration Error regularizer based on an expectation-maximization algorithm and add it to the fine-tuning loss. Experiments validate the proposed methods. The distinction between regimes matters because it changes the intervention: ordinary calibration-aware adaptation is supplemented by explicit error regularization as performance-oriented training progresses.
icml-2025-restoring-calibration-for-alig.tldr: Calibration-aware fine-tuning and an EM-based regularizer address overconfidence introduced by preference alignment across two calibration regimes.

paragraphs: SANA-1.5 addresses how to allocate computation when building and using text-to-image models. It extends a linear Diffusion Transformer with methods for growing a model, reducing its depth, and spending more computation during generation. Together, these methods provide different ways to accommodate available compute budgets.

For training, a depth-growth strategy scales the model from 1.6 billion to 4.8 billion parameters with substantially reduced computational requirements, alongside a memory-efficient 8-bit optimizer. For compression, block-importance analysis guides depth pruning to different model sizes with minimal quality loss. At inference, repeated sampling lets smaller models trade additional computation for quality comparable to larger models.

The reported GenEval text-image alignment score is 0.72, increasing to 0.80 with inference-time scaling; the paper reports this as a new state of the art on that benchmark. The contribution spans the model lifecycle: capacity can be expanded during training, reduced for deployment, or partly compensated for through additional sampling when generating images.
icml-2025-sana-1-5-efficient-scaling-of-.tldr: SANA-1.5 combines depth growth, pruning, and repeated sampling to improve text-to-image quality across training and inference compute budgets.

paragraphs: Adaptive optimizers use preconditioners to transform their updates, and the structure of those preconditioners affects memory and computation. This paper provides one analysis covering layerwise, diagonal, and Kronecker-factored choices. It treats both online regret minimization and offline convex optimization, bringing several established methods into a common theoretical framework.

The analysis recovers matching rates for diagonal AdaGrad, full-matrix AdaGrad, and AdaGrad-Norm. It also establishes an improved convergence rate for a one-sided Shampoo variant relative to original Shampoo. These results allow different structural choices to be assessed through shared reasoning rather than only as separate algorithms.

A central finding challenges the view that cheaper, more structured preconditioners are simply approximations whose goal should be to resemble full-matrix AdaGrad more closely. The authors show that structure can itself improve optimization: one-sided Shampoo can outperform full-matrix AdaGrad theoretically and experimentally while costing substantially less. This establishes a possible advantage for stronger structure, rather than a universal ranking of the methods.
icml-2025-structured-preconditioners-in-.tldr: A unified analysis shows that cheaper structured preconditioners can outperform fuller alternatives, with one-sided Shampoo providing a concrete example.

paragraphs: A language model can revise code in response to feedback, but that feedback must correctly identify problems and suggest useful changes. This paper studies how to train a critic specifically for that role. Its framework, CTRL, uses reinforcement learning to make critiques more effective at helping another model correct its code.

The training objective is correction performance for a fixed generator model, and the procedure does not require human supervision. This ties the critic’s learning directly to the usefulness of its feedback. The reported results show that trained critics improve pass rates and reduce compounding errors with both base generators and stronger generator models.

The authors also find that the critics can serve as accurate generative reward models. Repeated rounds of critique and revision provide a way to improve performance by spending more computation at test time. Across challenging code-generation benchmarks, the paper reports relative improvements of up to 106.1%. That maximum describes the evaluated gains, while the broader contribution is training feedback around its ability to enable successful correction.
icml-2025-teaching-language-models-to-cr.tldr: CTRL trains code critics through reinforcement learning to provide feedback that improves correction and supports iterative critique-and-revision.

paragraphs: Equivariant networks for three-dimensional modeling use tensor products to combine geometric features while preserving the required symmetry behavior. These operations can be expensive, motivating faster alternatives. This paper argues that comparing their speed requires understanding what each operation can represent, because different tensor products do not necessarily perform equivalent computations.

The authors introduce measures of expressivity and interactability to characterize those differences. Their analysis finds that reported speed improvements typically involve reduced expressivity. They also simplify the Gaunt tensor product implementation by operating directly on a spherical grid, preserving its asymptotic runtime while improving practical speed.

The spherical-grid approach is faster in their benchmarks and speeds actual training of the MACE interatomic potential by 30%. Systematic microbenchmarks additionally reveal large differences between theoretical runtime guarantees and measured performance. The results make architecture selection a joint question of representational ability and practical cost, with application-specific measurements needed to determine which operation offers the most useful tradeoff.
icml-2025-the-price-of-freedom-exploring.tldr: Tensor-product speedups often trade away expressivity, and practical benchmarks reveal performance differences that asymptotic runtime alone misses.

paragraphs: This paper connects several machine-learning trust concerns through a shared question: how much can particular data influence a trained model? It treats memorization, data poisoning, and copyright-related constraints in terms of differences in the outputs of a processing function, such as a training algorithm, when the relevant data influence changes.

The proposed framework, Data-Specific Indistinguishability, selects randomization tailored to the outcome differences being constrained. It relaxes classic Input-Independent Indistinguishability and aims to align the added noise closely with the specific trust requirement. The authors establish theoretical and algorithmic foundations using an optimal multivariate Gaussian mechanism.

They also show how to apply the framework to deep learning with black-box optimizers. Experiments on memorization mitigation, backdoor defense, and copyright protection support the efficiency and effectiveness of the noise mechanism. The contribution is a common mathematical approach for these data-influence constraints, together with a way to choose targeted randomization that provides provable guarantees within that formulation.
icml-2025-trustworthy-machine-learning-t.tldr: Data-Specific Indistinguishability tailors Gaussian randomization to particular data influences, providing a unified framework for several machine-learning trust guarantees.

paragraphs: An autonomous-driving anomaly detector must recognize unusual situations quickly as well as accurately. This paper places response time alongside accuracy as a central design objective. Its approach combines two camera inputs whose information is useful in different ways: event streams provide high temporal resolution, while RGB images supply spatial detail.

The proposed multimodal asynchronous hybrid network processes event-camera data with an asynchronous graph neural network. A convolutional neural network extracts spatial features from RGB images, and the system integrates the two. This combination is designed to capture rapid changes in the driving environment together with the visual structure needed to interpret them.

Experiments on benchmark datasets report better accuracy and response time than existing methods, with millisecond-level real-time performance. The findings support the value of combining event and image information when detection delay is part of the objective. The architectural contribution is the coordinated use of asynchronous temporal processing and image-based spatial processing to make anomaly detection both swift and precise.
icml-2025-when-every-millisecond-counts-.tldr: Combining event-camera streams with RGB images improves driving-anomaly detection accuracy and response time, achieving reported millisecond-level performance.
